response.query: What minimum device specifications, certification requirements, and secure data-transmission standards will participant devices and vendor partners be required to meet?
response.answer: Participant devices must meet ISO 26262 and ISO 21434 standards, and vendor partners must comply with EAR due diligence measures for advanced computing ICs. Secure data transmission requires adherence to relevant cybersecurity protocols.

results.content: # Key Requirements for Automotive SoC Design. Read on to learn more about the requirements to address each of these areas in your automotive SoC designs. AEC-Q100 provides failure mechanism-based stress test qualification for packaged automotive ICs. Given that automotive chips must operate under harsh conditions, stress testing while they are being designed can lead to more reliable automotive systems. Electronic design automation (EDA) and IP solutions vendors can provide automotive SoC designers with the technologies needed to achieve high levels of quality, reliability, safety, and security in their designs. Synopsys, for example, delivers automotive solutions spanning design and verification, implementation, signoff, and manufacturing/in-field operations to help designers comply with standards including ISO 26262 and ISO 21434. Ensuring that these chip designs meet quality, reliability, safety, and security requirements will help produce smarter, safer vehicles. Person Owned by, Controlled by, or Subject to the Jurisdiction or Direction of a Foreign Adversary](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/01/16/2025-00592/securing-the-information-and-communications-technology-and-services-supply-chain-connected-vehicles#h-45). In the ANPRM, BIS sought public comment to inform a rulemaking that would address the undue or unacceptable risks, as identified in Executive Order (E.O.) 13873, “Securing the Information and Communications Technology and Services Supply Chain,” [84 FR 22689](https://www.federalregister.gov/citation/84-FR-22689) (May 17, 2019), posed by a class of transactions that involve ICTS designed, developed, manufactured, or supplied by persons owned by, controlled by, or subject to the jurisdiction or direction of a foreign adversary and integral to connected vehicles. BIS received 101 comments on the NPRM.[[1](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/01/16/2025-00592/securing-the-information-and-communications-technology-and-services-supply-chain-connected-vehicles#footnote-1-p5363)]  Many commenters agreed with BIS's risk assessment of foreign adversary connected vehicle technology as described in Section IV of the NPRM and supported the decision to address these risks through supply chain regulation.
